title: Purgatory and the dead
hook: Catholics teach purification after death and pray for the dead; the Orthodox pray for the dead without that word; Protestants pray differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, images: icons, statues and plain white walls. Your line was what helps you pray.

Paul, writing to Timothy, remembers a man named Onesiphorus. When Paul was in chains in Rome, this man wasn't ashamed of him; he searched the city until he found him. Then Paul prays for him: "The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day." Paul greets the household of Onesiphorus, not the man himself, and some readers think he had already died. If so, this is Paul praying for the dead. What happens to those who have died is today's question.
screen: `A FRIEND WHO FOUND PAUL IN CHAINS.`
`MAY HE FIND MERCY IN THAT DAY.`

segments.voice: Catholics teach that some who die in God's grace are not yet fully ready to see God, and are purified after death. That purifying is called purgatory. It isn't a second chance, and it isn't a milder hell: those being purified are saved, and it ends in heaven. So Catholics pray for the dead, and have Masses offered for them. They point to Second Maccabees, a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. After a battle, Judas Maccabeus finds that fallen soldiers had carried idols, and he has prayers and a sacrifice offered so that their sin might be blotted out. They point, too, to Paul's picture of a builder whose work is tested by fire: "he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire." The Orthodox also pray for the dead, at memorial services where they sing memory eternal, and entrust them to God's mercy. But they don't use the word purgatory, or describe the state of the dead in the same detail. Protestant churches, following the Reformers, set purgatory aside. They teach that Christ's work is enough, and that those who die in him go to be with him. At Protestant funerals the dead are commended to God, and their lives given thanks for. This week walked through places where churches part ways: baptism, the table, Mary, the saints, images, and now the dead. On each, the differences are real, and honestly held. And under today's, Paul's short prayer for his friend still stands: may he find mercy.

Wait for a face to come, a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to, and say their name; remember one ordinary thing, the way they laughed, the food they made. If you pray, commend them to God's mercy in your tradition's words; if you don't, hold their memory gently, and thank them. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Purgatory. In Catholic teaching, the purifying of the saved after death, before they see God. The Orthodox and Protestants speak of the dead in other ways.
Your line: mercy after death. A friend, remembered in a prayer. Day one thousand one hundred six.
